# Mobile design

Rules for phone and tablet apps, judged on what renders. Apply the shared part and the section of each OS the app ships on; never carry one OS's conventions to the other.

## Shared core

Judge every rule on the rendered result, from the captures; the rules under Direction before code are the exception, checked as a plan in the worker's report or `DESIGN.md`, not on a render. `(behavior check)` marks a rule no capture can show (a file, a process, an input sequence): Worker.operations runs it and reports it, and nobody infers it from a still. `(preference)` marks taste: list it, do not repair it. A violation of any other rule is judged by this definition:

A discrepancy is material, and starts a repair whatever its size, when it affects acceptance, hierarchy or composition, legibility (cramped, overlapping, clipped or disappearing text), responsiveness at a viewport or size the criteria list, whether text and numbers state the content correctly (a title that misstates what it covers), accessibility, interaction correctness, adherence to a reference or obvious production quality; unnecessary text, headings, cards or badges are design defects. Only pure preference, with none of these effects, stays unrepaired: list it apart, marked optional.

A number is binding only where a platform guideline fixes it; every other number is a default, marked `(default)`, that the design may override with a stated reason.

Apply the skill's capture checklist on the final captures: the worker before reporting, the reviewer in its findings and the root in its own final pass. Check your own work as it takes shape, from captures wherever the environment can produce them. Report only checks actually run, and name each check not run.

### Direction before code

- When the brief leaves out the subject, the audience or the main job, confirm them with the user when one can answer, and otherwise state them as a proposal in the plan; remembered preferences or project context are a starting hint. The brief's own words outrank every avoid list below.
- Let the subject supply the look: its trade, materials and idiom decide the visual choices, and the brief's real content stays in the work from start to finish. A ferry timetable and a toddler's game should look nothing alike.
- Choose palette, type and layout on purpose and for this brief alone, accept visual risk when it earns its place, and treat each project as a chance to try something new instead of repeating what you do best.
- Sketch a plan before building: a small named palette (four to six colors, each with a value and a role), the type roles, a layout idea in a sentence, compared through rough ASCII wireframes, with how the content aligns (left, centered or justified), and two or three principles. Audit it with "would I make this for any similar product?" and the competitor test: drop an idea that still works with a competitor's name on it. Rewrite what fails, note what changed and why, and start coding only from the revised plan.
- Say whether this is a refinement, which preserves the existing design, or a redesign, which replaces it.

### Platform fidelity over invention

- Use the platform's own components, navigation and conventions unless the brief gives a reason not to, and brand through the layer the platform leaves open.
- Ported-from-a-website test: a fluent user of the platform never pauses at an off-spec control.
- Rules here are platform concepts. Detect the project's stack and map each rule onto it; never assume one.

### Design record

- Read `DESIGN.md` at the project root before UI work and create or update it after: platform and stack, direction, color roles, type roles, spacing and shape, components and states, do and don't, and a brief log of the options already tried, so later passes explore new ground. Note a changed decision instead of silently overwriting it. (behavior check)

### Spend boldness in one place

- Make one detail per screen the memorable one and keep the rest calm and restrained. Strip ornament that does nothing for the brief, and before finishing remove one accessory more, filling the gap with scale, real content or a real image so the screen is not left thin. (preference)
- A labeled gray placeholder beats drawn art or emoji used as icons. (preference)

### Structure and content

- A border, divider, outline, label, eyebrow or number belongs only where it tells the reader something true about the content. Numbers mark a real sequence (steps, a timeline) and nothing else, so confirm it is one first. An eyebrow over every heading, all-caps labels and labels that say nothing are decoration, not structure.
- With no real content in the brief, invent specific copy from the subject: generic words flatten a design as much as a generic layout does.

### Copy

- Interface text exists to help someone understand and act, so treat it as part of the design. Decide what the screen must convey and the shortest way to convey it, with one job for each piece of text.
- Speak in the user's terms, calling a thing what the user calls it ("saved searches", not "query presets"). Say what a thing is or does without selling it; concrete beats clever.
- Set text in sentence case unless the platform sets its own casing, leave out padding, keep the tone conversational and in step with the brand and its readers, and write in the active voice with everyday verbs.
- A control names its outcome ("Send invoice", not "Submit"), and each action carries one name from first label to confirmation: the Duplicate button leads to a "Duplicated" confirmation.
- When something fails or nothing is there yet, point the way. An error states what happened and how to recover, speaks as the interface and not as a person, and neither apologizes nor stays vague; an empty state invites the first action.

### Quality floor, unannounced

- Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 and non-text control contrast at least 3:1. Color is never the only signal, and the colors work together as a palette.
- Every state exists and is captured where reachable: hover or press, focus, disabled, loading, empty, error and long content.
- The system's reduced-motion, larger-text and high-contrast settings, where the platform has them, change the render; under reduced motion, movement becomes a fade or nothing.

## Shared mobile rules

- Adapt to the window size class, never the device, and name layout variants by class, not "tablet". Panes take the width they are given; extra width adds context and does not stretch content.
- System-bar and safe-area insets apply once per screen. Backgrounds draw edge to edge, and touch targets stay out of gesture areas. Symptom: content under a bar or doubled padding.
- Gestures supplement visible controls and never replace them.
- Refresh never clears existing content; skeletons are for the cold load only. Capture mid-refresh.
- Keyboard: "Next" moves through fields, and "Done" on the last dismisses the keyboard and keeps the text. (behavior check)
- After a refresh or rotation, focus and selection stay on the same item, not the same position. (behavior check)
- Haptics reach only the holder and sound reaches the room, so feedback scales with rarity. One action produces one feedback, never a doubled buzz or sound. (behavior check)
- Every interactive element has a label unique within its collection. A row reads as one announcement and exposes a multi-action row's actions by name. (behavior check)

## iOS and iPadOS

- Targets are 44×44 pt. 28×28 pt is the stated minimum for dense controls. Pad about 12 pt around bezeled and about 24 pt around unbezeled elements.
- Use the system text styles, 17 pt by default and 11 pt at least, with no light weights. Text scales to at least 200%, custom fonts included.
- At accessibility text sizes truncate as little as possible, allow as many lines as needed, stack rows vertically and scale meaningful icons with the text. Capture that size.
- Tab bars hold sections, never actions. Never hide or disable a tab, avoid a "More" overflow, and use single-word labels.
- A visible Back button stays, and the edge swipe is a shortcut. On iPad prefer the tab bar, which may become a sidebar of at most two levels.
- A sheet holds one scoped task at a time. Cancel goes leading and Done trailing, never Cancel, Done and Back together, and a swipe-dismiss that would lose changes asks first. (behavior check)
- Liquid Glass (iOS 26 and later): glass is the control and navigation layer, never the content layer, and custom glass is not stacked on glass. Use the regular variant by default and the clear variant only over rich media. Tint only the primary action's background, and strip custom bar backgrounds and borders. Corners are concentric: inner radius equals outer radius minus padding.
- iOS 27 guidance on scroll edges, sidebars, tab bars, menus, search and icons is not encoded here; judge those on a render of the target OS.
- Color is semantic. Every custom color has light, dark and increased-contrast variants.
- Aim for 7:1 on small text, and offer no in-app appearance switch. (preference)
- Common actions use system symbols matched to the text weight.
- Motion is purposeful, optional and cancelable; under Reduce Motion movement becomes a fade. Capture with the setting on.

## Android

- Window size classes in dp. Width: compact below 600, medium 600 to 839, expanded 840 to 1199, large 1200 to 1599, extra-large 1600 and up. Height: compact below 480, medium 480 to 899, expanded 900 and up. The layout is re-evaluated on every resize, fold or split-screen change. (behavior check)
- One primary navigation surface at a time. Compact uses a navigation bar. Medium uses a bar or a rail, by whether horizontal or vertical space matters more. Expanded and up use a rail. Prefer the expanded rail over a drawer, which Material 3 Expressive no longer recommends.
- Targets are at least 48×48 dp with 8 dp or more between them; pointer targets are at least 44 dp.
- Edge to edge is enforced from Android 15: content draws behind the system bars, bar icons keep contrast, interactive content is inset, and a scrim sits where content scrolls under a bar.
- Predictive back is on by default: the back swipe previews the destination and lands where the preview showed. Custom back behavior goes through the platform's back handling. (behavior check)
- Color and type use Material roles, never raw values. Type roles are Display, Headline, Title, Body and Label in large, medium and small; adjust line height and tracking before sizes. An "on" color sits on its paired fill, and container colors are fills, not text colors. Light and dark use the same roles. Contrast levels are standard, medium and high, and each is judged in light and dark.
- Choose components by behavior. Expressive motion is for a few moments and the rest stays calm (preference).

## Refuse list

Unless the brief asks for it:

- a card around every row, and a FAB for a minor action (preference)
- chips used as buttons
- a "Materialized" screen of radii and pastels (preference)
- iOS navigation patterns on Android, or Material navigation on iOS
- a hamburger drawer where an expanded rail fits
- a custom control where the system one exists (the ported-from-a-website test)

## Capture checklist

Capture each size class the brief targets (at least compact and one wider class). For each: light and dark, the largest standard and an accessibility text size, and reduced motion on. Add increased contrast on iOS, a refresh in progress, a sheet or back transition, and the keyboard open. Capture both OSes when the app ships on both.
